summary: Describes the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol, a cryptographically strong network authentication and key exchange mechanism based on a password. The password itself is not sent over the network.

plainLanguage.summary: Secure Remote Password (SRP) is a way to check a password over a network without ever sending the password. The host keeps a scrambled version of the password and a random salt instead of the password itself. While checking the password, both sides also compute a shared secret key, so the same exchange can start an encrypted session.

subtitle: Password authentication that never sends the password, and produces a shared key in the same exchange.

tldr.problem: Password-based authentication is hard to do securely: cleartext passwords can be sniffed, and challenge-response schemes can still be broken by guessing common passwords offline.
tldr.mechanism: SRP keeps a password verifier and a salt on the host, runs one Diffie-Hellman-style round so both sides compute the same session key, and then both sides prove they hold that key with a hash.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says SRP gives complete protection against passive and active attacks, needs no key server, no certificates and no long-term client keys, and can be dropped into an existing password login.

facts.label: Group modulus N
facts.value: a safe prime, N = 2q + 1 with q prime

today: RFC 2945 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. The document describes the SRP-SHA1 mechanism, points to a separate paper for the protocol itself, and notes that the same scheme can be used with other hash functions.

sections.title: Why Password Authentication Is Hard
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a problem with most Internet protocols: there is no secure authentication mechanism that is also easy to use. The problem is two-fold. Users like passwords they can remember, but most password-based systems give little protection even against passive attackers, especially when the password is weak and easily guessed.

Eavesdropping on a TCP/IP network is easy and effective against protocols that transmit passwords in the clear. Even so-called challenge-response techniques, such as the ones described in RFC 2095 and RFC 1760, which are designed to defeat simple sniffing attacks, can be compromised by a dictionary attack. There an attacker captures the messages exchanged during a legitimate run of the protocol and uses that information to verify a series of guessed passwords taken from a precompiled dictionary of common passwords. This works because users often choose simple, memorable passwords, which are also easy to guess.

Many existing mechanisms also require the password database on the host to be kept secret, because the password or a private hash of it is stored there and would compromise security if revealed. The RFC says that approach often degenerates into security through obscurity, and goes against the UNIX convention of keeping a public password file whose contents can be revealed without destroying system security.

SRP meets the strictest requirements laid down in RFC 1704 for a non-disclosing authentication protocol. It offers complete protection against both passive and active attacks, and does so efficiently using a single Diffie-Hellman-style round of computation, which makes it feasible for interactive and non-interactive authentication. Because it keeps its security with low-entropy passwords, it can be integrated into existing user applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords are hard to protect. Sending one in the clear lets anyone on the network read it, and schemes that avoid that can still be broken offline by guessing common words. The RFC also argues that the host should not have to protect a secret password file, because a leaked file of password hashes is enough to start guessing.

sections.title: Conventions for Bytes and Integers
sections.content:
The RFC describes an abstract protocol that can be fitted to any application; the format of the messages, including padding, is left to the implementor. One issue is worth specifying, because SRP does algebraic operations on its messages while Internet protocols are byte-oriented: how integers are converted to strings of bytes and back.

An n-byte string S is converted to an integer as i = S[n-1] + 256 * S[n-2] + 256^2 * S[n-3] + ... + 256^(n-1) * S[0]. In human terms, the string of bytes is the integer written in base 256 with the most significant digit first. When converting back to a string, S[0] must be non-zero, and padding is treated as a separate process. If an implementation needs to pad a string that represents an integer, the RFC recommends using zero bytes added to the beginning of the string, because converting back to an integer automatically discards leading zero bytes, which makes this scheme less prone to error.

The SHA hash function in this document means the SHA-1 message digest algorithm. The protocol itself is sometimes called SRP-3 for historical reasons; the fuller description is in a separate paper.
sections.plainLanguage: SRP does maths on its messages, but the network carries bytes. The RFC fixes one conversion rule: a string of bytes is read as a number written in base 256, most significant digit first. Padding, if any, goes in front as zero bytes.

sections.title: Password Verifiers and Group Parameters
sections.content:
The host stores user passwords as triplets of the form { <username>, <password verifier>, <salt> }. Password entries are generated as follows.

<salt> = random()
x = SHA(<salt> | SHA(<username> | ":" | <raw password>))
<password verifier> = v = g^x % N

The | symbol is string concatenation, ^ is exponentiation and % is the integer remainder operation. Most implementations perform the exponentiation and the remainder in a single stage, to avoid generating unwieldy intermediate results. The 160-bit output of SHA is implicitly converted to an integer before it is operated upon.

The values of N and g must be agreed upon by the two parties. They can be set in advance, or the host can supply them to the client, in which case it should send them in the first message along with the salt. For maximum security, N should be a safe prime, a number of the form N = 2q + 1 where q is also prime. The value g should be a generator modulo N, which means that for any X where 0 < X < N there is a value x for which g^x % N == X.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of the password, the host keeps a verifier and a random salt. The verifier is produced by hashing the password with the username and the salt, then raising a fixed number g to that hash. The verifier is useless to an attacker on its own: turning a guessed password into a matching verifier costs an expensive modular exponentiation.

sections.title: The SRP-SHA1 Exchange
sections.content:
Authentication is generally initiated by the client. The client sends the username, and the host replies with the salt stored under that name. The client then generates a random number a, raises g to that power modulo N, and sends A = g^a % N. The host does the same with a random b, adds the stored verifier, and returns B = (v + g^b) % N. Both sides then construct the shared session key from their own values.

p = <raw password>
x = SHA(s | SHA(U | ":" | p))
S = (B - g^x) ^ (a + u * x) % N       S = (A * v^u) ^ b % N
K = SHA_Interleave(S)                 K = SHA_Interleave(S)

The parameter u is a 32-bit unsigned integer taken from the first 32 bits of the SHA1 hash of B, most significant bit first. The client MUST abort authentication if B % N is zero. The host MUST abort the authentication attempt if A % N is zero, and MUST send B after receiving A from the client, never before.

At that point both sides have a common session key that is not known to an outside party. To finish authentication they must prove to each other that their keys are identical. The client sends M = H(H(N) XOR H(g) | H(U) | s | A | B | K). The server computes M with its own K and compares it against the client's value. If they do not match, the server MUST abort and signal an error before it answers the client's challenge, because not doing so could compromise the security of the user's password. If the server receives a correct response, it issues its own proof, H(A | M | K), which the client checks with its own K.

The transactions described here do not necessarily correspond one to one with real protocol messages. The RFC shows how the flows can be consolidated into fewer messages: the client sends U and A together, the host replies with s and B, the client sends the proof M, and the host answers with H(A | M | K).
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange has four steps. The client sends its name and a number built from a random value. The host replies with the salt and a similar number that includes the stored verifier. From these, both sides compute the same session key without ever sending the password. Finally, each side sends a hash of the key to prove it reached the same value.

sections.title: Interleaved SHA and Other Hash Functions
sections.content:
The SHA_Interleave function generates a session key that is twice as long as the 160-bit output of SHA1. To compute it, remove all leading zero bytes from the input. If the length of the resulting string is odd, also remove the first byte, and call the result T. Extract the even-numbered bytes into a string E and the odd-numbered bytes into a string F, so that E = T[0] | T[2] | T[4] | ... and F = T[1] | T[3] | T[5] | .... Both E and F are exactly half the length of T. Hash each one with regular SHA1 to get G and H, then interleave the two hashes back together as result = G[0] | H[0] | G[1] | H[1] | ... | G[19] | H[19]. The result is 40 bytes, or 320 bits, long.

SRP can be used with hash functions other than SHA. If the hash function produces output of a different length than SHA, which is 20 bytes, it may change the length of some of the messages in the protocol, but the fundamental operation is unaffected. Earlier versions of the SRP mechanism used the MD5 hash function. Keyed hash transforms are also recommended, and one possible construction uses HMAC, using K to key the hash in each direction instead of concatenating it with the other parameters.

Any hash function used with SRP should produce an output of at least 16 bytes and have the property that small changes in the input cause significant nonlinear changes in the output.
sections.plainLanguage: The session key is built by hashing the shared secret twice, in two halves, and putting the two results back together in alternating order. That gives a 320-bit key from a 160-bit hash. SRP also works with other hash functions, as long as the hash produces at least 16 bytes and mixes its input well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The whole document describes an authentication and key-exchange system that protects passwords and exchanges keys across an untrusted network. The system improves security by removing the need to send cleartext passwords and by enabling encryption through its key-exchange mechanism.

The private values for a and b correspond roughly to the private values in a Diffie-Hellman exchange and have similar constraints of length and entropy. Implementations may choose to increase the length of the parameter u, as long as both client and host agree, but it is not recommended that it be shorter than 32 bits.

SRP was designed not only to counter casual password sniffing, but also to prevent a determined attacker with a dictionary of passwords from guessing passwords using captured network traffic. The protocol also resists active network attacks, and implementations can use the exchanged keys to protect the session against hijacking and to provide confidentiality.

SRP also lets the host store passwords in a form that is not directly useful to an attacker. Even if the password database were publicly revealed, an attacker would still need an expensive dictionary search to obtain any password, because the exponential computation required to validate a guess is far more time-consuming than the hash most UNIX systems use. Hosts are still advised to do their best to keep their password files secure.
sections.plainLanguage: SRP is meant to resist a passive attacker who records traffic, an active attacker who interferes with the exchange, and an attacker who has stolen the password file. Checking a guessed password against the stored verifier takes an expensive modular exponentiation, so a stolen file does not quickly give up the passwords.

items.title: No cleartext password
items.text: The password never crosses the network.

items.title: No long-term client keys
items.text: Clients need no stored or managed keys.

items.title: No key server or certificates
items.text: Trusted key servers and certificate infrastructure are not required.

items.title: One round of computation
items.text: A single Diffie-Hellman-style round also produces the session key.
